headline: A bomb kills three outside a Moscow restaurant

sources.title: Female Bomber Kills at Least 3, Injures 21 Near Moscow Restaurant
Moscow mayor calls Saturday's deadly bomb attack on a restaurant a 'terrorist act'
Three dead including female bomber in Moscow restaurant attack
Three people killed, at least 21 wounded in Moscow restaurant bombing, Russian officials say (video, AP Archive)

chunks.text: A [[homemade]] bomb {{went off}} outside an Italian restaurant in central Moscow on Saturday evening, August 1. A woman carrying the [[device]] tried to walk in through the front door. A [[security guard]] {{stepped in}} and {{turned her away}}, and the bomb exploded on the street [[a moment later]]. Three people were killed, the woman herself, the guard and one customer. Twenty-one others were [[wounded]], six of them [[seriously]].

verbs.wrong: To be carried into a building
verbs.why: A firework can go off with a loud crack, and a firecracker can go off without warning if someone drops it. In Moscow, a homemade bomb went off outside a restaurant just seconds after a guard stopped a woman at the door.

verbs.correct: To get involved in order to stop something
verbs.wrong: To hold the door open for a customer
verbs.why: A teacher can step in before a fight turns physical, and a manager sometimes has to step in during a crisis. A security guard stepped in just before the woman reached the restaurant door, moments before the bomb exploded outside.

verbs.correct: To refuse to let someone enter
verbs.wrong: To search a person at the door
verbs.why: A full restaurant sometimes has to turn away customers at the door, and a clinic may turn away patients without an appointment. A security guard turned the woman away just before the bomb exploded on the street outside.

chunks.text: The restaurant [[sits on]] Kudrinskaya Square, under one of the seven tall [[Stalin-era]] towers that stand around the city. It had been closed that evening for a [[private event]]. Russia's national [[anti-terrorism committee]] is {{looking into}} the attack but has {{put out}} very little. It has not named the woman, the [[victims]] or any [[suspect]], and it has not {{ruled out}} [[the possibility that]] she did not know what she was carrying.

verbs.wrong: To watch a place from outside
verbs.why: Police often look into complaints before deciding whether to open a full case, and journalists look into a story before publishing it. Russia's anti-terrorism committee is looking into the bombing but has shared very few details so far.

verbs.correct: To release information to the public
verbs.wrong: To send officers to a crime scene
verbs.why: Companies put out statements after a crisis, and weather agencies put out warnings before a storm. Investigators have put out very little so far, not even the name of the woman who carried the bomb.

verbs.correct: To decide that something is not possible
verbs.wrong: To question a witness about something
verbs.why: Doctors rule out a serious illness after running tests, and police sometimes rule out early guesses in a case. The police have not ruled out the chance that the woman herself did not know what she was carrying.

chunks.text: Nobody has {{come forward}} to say they organized it. The mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, called the [[blast]] a brutal [[terrorist act]] and said those [[behind it]] would be found. [[Beyond that]], almost nothing [[official]] has been said, and the space has filled with [[guesswork]]. Some Russian [[war bloggers]] blamed Ukraine without offering [[proof]], and Kyiv did not answer them. One Russian newspaper suggested the bomb may have been detonated [[from a distance]] by somebody else. So far nothing public {{points to}} any single answer. Russians have {{looked back}} to a café bombing in the same city in 2023, when a woman who carried a hidden bomb to a public event was later [[sentenced to]] 27 years in prison.

verbs.correct: To make yourself known in public
verbs.wrong: To arrive at a place before others
verbs.why: A witness sometimes comes forward months after a crime, and a person with new information may come forward once they feel safe. Nobody has come forward yet to say they organized the Moscow bombing.

verbs.correct: To suggest that something is true
verbs.wrong: To name a person in an official list
verbs.why: Small clues sometimes point to who is responsible for a crime, and test results can point to an answer before doctors confirm it. So far, nothing public points to any single answer about who planted the bomb.

verbs.correct: To think about something in the past
verbs.why: People often look back on their school years with a smile, and historians look back at earlier events to find patterns. Russians have looked back to a similar 2023 cafe bombing that also used a hidden device.

chunks.text: What is left is a short list of things nobody can {{clear up}} yet. Investigators must {{track down}} whoever built the device and whoever chose the place and the hour. They are {{holding back}} most of what they know, which is normal early in a case like this but [[leaves everyone else guessing]]. The [[square]] is open again, the tower still stands above it, and a restaurant that was closed for a quiet evening has become the address of the worst attack in the [[capital]] this year.

verbs.correct: To explain something that is confusing
verbs.wrong: To close a street to traffic
verbs.why: A short phone call can clear up a misunderstanding fast, and one clear test can clear up a doctor's doubt. Investigators still cannot clear up who built the bomb or why that restaurant was chosen.

verbs.wrong: To follow a person without being seen
verbs.why: Detectives track down missing people after a long search, and collectors sometimes track down a rare item for years. Investigators must track down whoever built the device and whoever chose the time and place.

verbs.wrong: To close a case without an answer
verbs.why: A company sometimes holds back the true cost of a repair, and a witness may hold back details out of fear. Investigators are holding back most of what they know, which is normal early in a serious case.

mainIdea.s: A bomb went off outside a Moscow restaurant after a security guard turned away the woman carrying it. Three people died, twenty-one were hurt, and no group has come forward to claim it.
mainIdea.why: A security guard stepped in and turned the woman away before she reached the door. The bomb then exploded outside, killing three and wounding twenty-one people.

mainIdea.s: Outside a Moscow restaurant, a bomb killed three people after a guard stopped a woman at the entrance. Russian authorities have officially confirmed that a foreign government ordered the attack.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no suspect or group has been confirmed. War bloggers guessed that Ukraine was behind it, but they offered no proof and Kyiv did not respond.

mainIdea.s: A different bombing hit a Moscow cafe back in 2023, when a woman carried a hidden device inside. A court later gave the bomber a sentence of 27 years in a Russian prison for that crime.
mainIdea.why: This story is about an earlier 2023 cafe bombing in Moscow, not the restaurant attack from August 2026.

lines.text: There was a bombing in central Moscow on Saturday. A homemade bomb {{went off}} outside an Italian restaurant. Three people were killed.

A woman carrying the device tried to enter through the front door. A security guard {{stepped in}} and {{turned her away}}. The bomb exploded on the street [[moments later]]. The woman, the guard, and one customer died, and 21 people were wounded.
The guard probably saved many lives.
Almost certainly. The restaurant was closed for a private event that evening.
Nobody knows. No one has {{come forward}} to claim it, and investigators have {{put out}} very little. They haven't named the woman or any suspect.

Guesses, not facts. Some war bloggers blamed Ukraine without proof. One newspaper suggested the bomb was detonated from a distance, and officials haven't {{ruled out}} that the woman didn't know what she was carrying.
She might not have known? [[That's chilling]].
It has happened before. People {{looked back}} to a 2023 cafe bombing in the same city, where a woman carried a hidden bomb to a public event.
The anti-terrorism committee is {{looking into}} it. Investigators must {{track down}} whoever built the device and chose the place. So far, nothing public {{points to}} a single answer.
Why so quiet about the details?
They're {{holding back}} most of what they know, which is normal [[early on]], but it leaves everyone guessing. There's a long list of things nobody can {{clear up}} yet.
A quiet evening that became the worst attack in the capital this year.
